title: Further Applications of Newton's Laws: Friction, Drag, and Elasticity

variables.meaning: magnitude of the friction force, which is parallel to the contact surface and always opposes motion or attempted motion
magnitude of static friction, the force between two systems that are in contact and are not moving relative to one another
the largest static friction the surfaces can supply; once the applied force exceeds it, the object moves
magnitude of kinetic friction, the force between two systems that are in contact and moving relative to one another
magnitude of the normal force, the force perpendicular to the contact surface between the systems
the force applied parallel to the surface, which static friction answers with an equal and opposite force until the object breaks away
coefficient of static friction, which depends on both of the materials in contact and carries no units
coefficient of kinetic friction, which is less than the coefficient of static friction for the same two materials
the weight of the skier, which the coordinate system of the slope splits into a component perpendicular to the slope and a component along it
the component of the weight perpendicular to the slope, equal in magnitude to the normal force, so that there is no motion perpendicular to the slope
the component of the weight along the slope, which is larger than the friction and so accelerates the skier down it
the angle the slope makes with the horizontal
the mass of the system whose weight presses the two surfaces together
the acceleration due to gravity, which turns the mass resting on the surface into a weight
magnitude of the drag force on an object moving through a fluid, which always opposes the motion
the drag coefficient, a dimensionless number determined empirically in a wind tunnel, which depends on the shape of the object
the area of the object facing the fluid
the density of the fluid the object moves through, which for air is 1.21 kg/m³
the speed of the object through the fluid, which the drag force depends on
the terminal velocity, the constant speed a falling object reaches when the drag force has grown equal to its weight
the constant 0.5CρA, which gathers the shape, the size and the fluid into one number so that the drag force is bv²
the mass of the falling object, whose weight the drag force grows to match
the acceleration due to gravity, which gives the falling object the weight mg
magnitude of the drag force given by Stokes' law, which holds for a very small object moving slowly or in a medium denser than air
the radius of the small object that Stokes' law applies to
the viscosity of the fluid, measured in kilograms per meter per second
the force applied to the object, which changes its shape rather than its motion
the deformation, the change in length the force produces
a proportionality constant that depends on the shape and the composition of the object and on the direction of the force
the original length of the wire or rod, before the force is applied
the cross-sectional area of the wire or rod, which is πr² for a cylinder of radius r
Young's modulus, the elastic modulus for a change in length, which depends on the substance; a material with a large Y deforms little for a given tension or compression
the shear modulus, which sets the sideways deformation that a shearing force produces
the bulk modulus, which sets the change in volume that a force per unit area applied evenly inward on all surfaces produces
the shear deformation, which is perpendicular to the original length rather than parallel to it
the change in volume produced by a force applied evenly inward on every surface
the original volume of the object, before it is compressed
the weight hung from the guitar string or from the nail, which is the force that deforms it
the radius of the rod, wire or nail, from which the cross-sectional area πr² is found
the mass whose weight deforms the object
